title: Before winter: 6 jobs for older houses and holiday lets
tips: Clear gutters and downpipes
Once the leaves are down. Overflowing gutters soak the wall behind them, and that shows up as damp inside.
Touch up bare timber
Check windows, doors and fascias on the south and west sides. Bare wood in a salt wind rots fast.
Check the sealant round baths and showers
Black or split silicone lets water into the floor below. Cheap to redo, expensive to ignore.
Keep air moving in empty lets
Leave the heating on low and trickle vents open, or condensation turns to mould by spring.
Lag pipes in lofts and outbuildings
A burst pipe in an empty house can run for days before anyone notices.
Get drains and treatment plants seen to now
Before the wet months, not in the middle of them.
caption:
Six jobs worth doing before the weather turns, especially in older houses and lets that sit empty over winter.

title: Building on a slope? 5 things to sort before the first dig
tips: Find out what's under you
Soil, rock and water decide the foundations. On steep plots an engineer's design is money well spent.
Plan the water first
Where rain and run-off go matters more than anything else on a slope. Drainage first, building second.
Retaining walls are structures
Anything holding back a real weight of ground needs designing, not guessing. Gabions and reinforced concrete each have their place.
Work out access early
If a lorry can't reach, concrete and materials go in by dumper, barrow or pump. Price that in from the start.
Get the order right
Walls and drainage go in before the frame, so the site stays workable through a wet winter.
caption:
Most plots round the estuary slope, and the work that goes in before anything is built decides how well the rest goes.

title: Thinking about a raised deck? Check these first
tips: Height
Under permitted development, a deck more than 30cm above the ground needs planning permission. On a sloping garden that's most of them.
Conservation areas and listed buildings
Parts of Fowey are a conservation area, and listed buildings need consent for most changes. Check before you design.
How much of the garden it covers
Decks, sheds and outbuildings together can't cover more than half the land around the original house without permission.
What it stands on
Posts on concrete pads dug below the topsoil, with a braced frame. Not posts sitting on the surface.
Sea air
Treated or naturally durable timber and stainless fixings, or it'll look tired in a few winters.
caption:
A raised deck can make a sloping garden usable, but check the rules before you get your heart set on a design.

This is general guidance; your council has the final say. If you'd like us to check yours, send us a message.

title: 6 questions to ask a builder before you say yes
tips: Are you insured?
Ask to see their public liability cover.
Can I have the quote written out by stage?
So you can see what's included, and what each part costs.
Who deals with planning and Building Regulations?
It should be clear from the start, and written into the quote.
Who does the electrics and gas?
Registered trades, and you should get the certificates at the end.
How will you keep me updated?
Especially if you're away. Regular photos beat surprise phone calls.
What's the payment schedule?
Stage payments against work done, not large sums up front.
caption:
Good questions to ask any builder, us included. A good one will be glad you asked.

title: 5 tools that keep a build on track
tips: A stage-by-stage plan
Written down before we start, so everyone knows what happens when, and what it costs.
A moisture meter
We check timber, screed and walls are dry enough before anything is closed in or finished.
A laser level
Floors, worktops and decks set out level once, not corrected later.
A shared photo thread
Progress photos every week, so owners who live away can see it without driving down.
A snagging list at handover
We walk round together and write down anything to finish, then sign it off.
caption:
Good building is mostly good organisation. These are the tools that stop small problems turning into big ones.
